I can provide sources for anything that sounds questionable from major sites and scientific journals.

  • Our regulatory agencies don't uniquely regulate GMOs. A company that engineers a new potato can go straight from the lab to the market, and sell it as just a potato, if they're already approved to sell potatoes. The GMO consultation from the FDA is purely voluntary and even then is basically a checklist. The EPA regulations only refer to a tiny subset of inventions related to invasive critters that nobody's doing anyhow. We're relying on the good ethics of corporations to not do anything bad.

  • The benefits of GMOs are negligible. The way things like increased yield are justified is by comparing undeveloped countries before and after given access to modern farming technology and genetically engineered seed. The former is where all the gains come from, the latter gets all the credit. Compare the yield of non-gmo vs gmo where farming technology is normalized and there is no benefit. One of the first comprehensive studies a few years back compared non-gmo yield in a few western european countries to gmo yield in the US. Our yield was actually slightly lower.

  • Along with the above, pesticide usage has increased. Insecticide usage is slightly down, but herbicide usage (almost all glyphosate related stuff) is through the roof as nature has ironically begin to naturally develop glyphosate resistant weeds and the like meaning you need to pour more of the stuff to get the same effect.

  • GMOs, like many markets in the US, are monopolized by a small handful of huge companies. As a result of this the genetic homogeneity of our agriculture has greatly increased. Plant disease happens. Plant disease + genetic homogeneity is a bad combination.
